title: Ayodhya Kanda: The Crown and the Wilderness
body:
Ayodhya Kanda: The Crown and the Wilderness

13. Dasharatha-vachana-palaka Rama
14. Tyakta-rajyabhiseka Rama
15. Kaikeyi-priya-putra Rama
16. Priyangu-bhratri-yukta Rama
17. Chitra-kutanilaya-nivasa Rama
18. Bharata-prarthita-paduka-dhari Rama

The Poison of Jealousy and Manthara's Evil Counsel

Twelve happy years passed in Ayodhya. As King Dasharatha felt the weight of old age, he decided to crown Rama as the heir apparent. The citizens of Ayodhya were ecstatic, for Rama's justice, mercy, and virtue had won every heart. But this joy was shattered by a single, bitter mind. Manthara, the hunchback maidservant of Queen Kaikeyi, was consumed by jealousy. She rushed to Kaikeyi's chambers, finding her genuinely pleased by the news of Rama's coronation, and began to drip toxic counsel into her ear.
We must pause and look closely at this moment. Kaikeyi was not a wicked woman; she loved Rama as her own son, even more than Bharata. But under the constant, manipulative whispers of Manthara, her noble nature slowly crumbled. Manthara warned her that once Rama took the throne, Kausalya would become the supreme queen and treat Kaikeyi as a slave, while Bharata would be exiled or worse. Jealousy is a fire that consumes the vessel that contains it. Kaikeyi yielded to these fears, entering the sulking room in soiled garments to demand the two boons Dasharatha had granted her long ago when she saved his life on a celestial battlefield. Her demands were brutal: Bharata must be crowned king, and Rama must be banished to the dangerous Dandaka forest for fourteen years.

The Agony of the King and Rama's Consolation to his Mother

The heartbroken king was shattered. He fell at Kaikeyi's feet, weeping and pleading with her to spare his beloved son, but she remained cold and unshakable, reminding him that a king who breaks his given word destroys the very foundation of truth. When Rama entered the chambers and saw his father collapsed in silent agony, he did not utter a single word of anger or resentment. With absolute calm and self-control, he accepted his stepmother's reluctant decree. To Rama, the kingdom was nothing compared to preserving his father's honor and the sanctity of truth.
When Rama broke the news of his banishment to Queen Kausalya, she fell to the ground like a cut tree, weeping in inconsolable grief: 'How can a mother endure the exile of her innocent, golden child to the dangerous woods? If you must go, let me follow you as a shadow.' Rama gently lifted her, speaking words of profound moral clarity: 'My beloved mother, a wife's primary duty is to remain by her husband's side, especially in his hour of deepest grief. My father is completely broken by his own word. If you leave him now, you will destroy him. Your dharma is to stay here, comforting him and guiding the court in my absence. Fourteen years will pass like a single night, and I will return to your arms.' His words completely pacified her grief, anchoring her heart in the steady anchor of moral duty.

The Exile and the Great Sacrifice of Bharata

Sita and Lakshmana insisted on accompanying Rama. As they walked toward the edge of the kingdom, they arrived at the banks of the Ganges River, where they met Guha, the chief of the tribal boatmen. Guha was deeply moved by the sight of the prince wearing garments of bark, his feet dusty from travel. He offered his entire territory and his services to Rama, but Rama embraced him warmly, declining his hospitality: 'My duty is to live as an ascetic in the forest, not to enjoy royal treatment in a new land.' Guha wept as he ferried them across the deep, silent river, watching until their figures disappeared into the dark woods of Chitrakoota.
Meanwhile, Bharata, who had been away visiting his maternal uncle, returned to a city of shadows. When he learned of his mother's scheming, his father's death, and his brother's exile, he was filled with intense grief and fury. He publicly rebuked Kaikeyi, refusing to profit from her wicked plots. Refusing to sit on the throne, he gathered the citizens and the army and set out into the wild forest to find Rama and bring him back.
He found Rama in the quiet woods of Chitrakoota. Bharata fell at his brother's feet, pleading with him to return and take the crown that was rightfully his. But Rama gently but firmly refused: 'Our father's word is sacred. I must complete the fourteen years of exile to fulfill his vow. You must return and rule Ayodhya to protect the people.' Seeing that Rama's resolve was unshakable, Bharata made a beautiful, noble sacrifice. He requested Rama's padukas—his wooden sandals—and placed them on his head. He vowed: 'I will place these sandals upon the throne of Ayodhya. I will live as an ascetic outside the city walls, ruling only as your deputy. If you do not return the very day the fourteen years end, I will walk into a fire.' Rama embraced him with deep emotion, and Bharata returned to Ayodhya, leaving the three companions to journey deeper into the southern forests.
